title: An Introduction to Rāga Khamāj
summary: A profile table for Khamāj (its own thāṭ, hexatonic up and heptatonic down, Ga–Ni vādī–saṃvādī, playful in mood). Then how learning grows (imitation, the guru's grace, practice, good company), copying songs heard by ear, and the start of Pathak ji's sound-notation: write the syllables by length and dot each rise and fall.

blocks.text: By practising [in] 16 mātrās (beats), the ability to make tāns (fast runs) oneself can also come.

As you wish, you can play any two or more tāns by joining them one after another without a break. If, in each of the three parts of a tihāī, tāns of equal mātrās are joined and played in the proper number of mātrās, it will be called a camatkārik (astonishing) tān. Usually the same rule applies to cakkardār (circling) tāns too. For special knowledge, one should take refuge with a guru who is an expert in tāla.

blocks.verse:
दृष्ट श्रुतानाम् परिशीलनेन श्रीमद् गुरुणामनुकम्पया च।
अभ्यास सद्भाव सुसंगततैश्च पुष्यन्ति विद्याः सलुसाधकानाम्।१४९।
blocks.text: Through close study of what has been seen and heard, through the kindness of revered gurus, and through practice, goodwill and good company, the learning of practitioners indeed flourishes.

For the creation of any vidyā (learning) takes place for every living being even before birth, in the form of saṃskāra (ingrained disposition). After that, [the question is] in what order that saṃskāra is found to develop. In this context the above śloka sets out that a child with saṃskāra is by nature an imitator; whatever subjects pass along the path of his senses, he keeps taking them in as seen or heard.

When that child grows a little older, the saṃskāra shown in his actions impresses his mother and father. Then, when he is taken to an illustrious guru suited to that same saṃskāra, the guru too, seeing his saṃskāra, becomes pleased even without any service [from him], and that very pleasure, becoming a blessing, makes that saṃskāra stronger still.

Later, in adolescence, he becomes engaged in abhyāsa (practice) under the guidance of the guru. By the strength of practice, that practitioner (sādhaka) wins over the many other bad saṃskāras of the world without effort, just as a two-wheeled bicycle, moving in a set direction under the guidance of its rider, seems to have forgotten how to fall this way and that. Then the peace of mind gained from the yoga of practice in the same way gives rise to sadbhāva (goodwill). Goodwill brings that practitioner together with those who appreciate merit, in whose company he moves forward towards ever greater progress.

Sometimes, when he begins to enjoy the charming honour that has come to him without offering it to the guru, a veil of ego spreads like mist between the guru's grace and the practitioner; then it is good company that removes it.
If the grace of the Lord can have a visible form, it is good company itself.

Thus, from birth to maturity, this is the order in which learning grows strong - (1) anukaraṇa (imitation) (2) gurukṛpā (the guru's grace) (3) abhyāsa (practice) (4) sadbhāva (goodwill) (5) susaṅgati (good company) (6) ānanda (bliss)
Now, for the benefit of those imitating practitioners who do not get the shelter of a guru's grace, the following śloka is presented.

blocks.verse:
श्रुतगीतगते नादे ध्यानयोगेन भाषते।
आरोहादि गुणग्रामः सोऽनुकार्यो मुहुर्मुहः।१५०।
blocks.text: The group of qualities such as ascent that shines forth, through the discipline of attention, in the nāda (musical sound) of songs one has heard is to be imitated again and again.

That is, in songs one has heard, the group of the various qualities of nāda (musical sound) that appears through the union of attention and is pictured in the mind should be imitated, trying again and again.

For only that can be played on an instrument which is pictured in the antaḥkaraṇa (inner mind) (first in the antar [the heart], then in the jantar [the instrument]). If the picture in the inner mind is blurred, making it clear with the help of listening is also a part of sādhanā (practice). If even then there is doubt about its clarity, that picture should be drawn on paper by the method given below. Just as it seems right to eat kheer and other foods cooked in a big vessel such as a bhagonā (cooking pot) after serving them out in measured portions into small vessels such as a thālī (plate), in the same way a picture of the notes, taken out of the bulk pictured in the world of the mind and out of the world of books and set down on paper, is more beneficial for practitioners; otherwise, along with the benefit, many faults may also arise.
Therefore we shall think it proper to take some part of the notation quoted in music treatises, which we can grasp easily, transfer it onto paper and then onto the bānsurī.

If the notation printed in a book is difficult, it can be made simple with the help of some musician. If the notation is difficult, the only reason is that the notation-writer has paid attention to the subtlety of the song and has wanted to write the notation honestly. Why should he feel pity for the weakness of the practitioner? That pity is the guru's dharma (duty). If hotel food is tasty, it can also be harmful for a sick person. In such a situation, if a sensible sick person is caught [there], he should wash the spicy vegetables in water and then eat them. In the same way, by removing elements such as kaṇ (grace notes), mīṇḍ (glides) and dugun (double tempo) from the difficult notations of film songs pleasing to the ear, the song becomes plain and simple.

blocks.verse:
स्वरशास्त्र विहीनानाम् जिज्ञासूनां हिताय वै।
लिख्यते नाद संकेतो स्वर शास्त्र धियाऽधुना।१५१।
blocks.text: Now, for the benefit of seekers who lack the science of svaras, a nāda saṃketa (sound-notation) is written down with an understanding of that science.
That is, a method of picturing notes on a scientific basis is being presented here. It is generally more useful for those practitioners who are unacquainted with svaralipi (notation).
(1) The natural mātrā (length) of the syllables in any song is fixed -

On the basis of chanda śāstra (the science of metre) there are two kinds of vowels (svara varṇa), guru (long) and laghu (short). Consonants do not have a mātrā of their own; the mātrā of the vowels standing around them governs their mātrā. Guru syllables are those whose pronunciation takes more time, such as long ā, long ī and so on. Laghu syllables are those whose mātrā takes less time, such as short i, short u. Besides these, a laghu with anusvāra, with visarga, or followed by a halant [consonant] is also guru, such as dil, śak, vil and so on. A short vowel standing before a conjunct consonant is also guru. If a singer has sung some guru as laghu, let that be taken as an exception. New practitioners should ignore the exception, adopt the general rule, and attend only to the natural mātrā of words, and by this same rule they should practise writing the mātrās of many songs and poems. For example, if we write any caupāī of the Rāmāyaṇa in its natural mātrās, half a caupāī will come to just 16 mātrās.
For example - dī - na da |  yā - la vi | ra da saṃ - | hā - rī - |
ha ra hunā | - tha ma ma | saṃ - ka ṭa | bhā - rī - |

blocks.text: (2) When we have written the song bound in mātrās, then, understanding the rise, fall and pause of the notes within them, write them as signs by putting a dot above or below those same mātrās, for example - ham - ko mȧ na kị̄ śȧ - ktị dė - nā | If a mātrā is higher than the mātrā before it, a dot should be put above, and if it is lower, below.

In songs being heard or already heard, these three actions are mostly perceived: the note going up, coming down, and staying steady. Among these, where the note changes along with a syllable, that change is easy to understand; but the change is harder to understand by hearing where one guru (long) syllable stands on some note and its ākār (sustained vowel) goes to another note. Therefore more care is needed in hearing and understanding guru syllables.

(3) Keeping the above points in mind, to bring out on the bānsurī a song one has heard, the practitioner should sit in a clean and solitary place, write down some one desired song with its mātrās, and himself put the dot signs on its mātrās, taking the map [of its melody] as the basis. Let it be kept in mind that he should take a small part of the song and reflect again and again on each syllable, then, starting from some one note, play one mātrā further at a time. If the mental picture is not satisfied with the note of some mātrā, he should change that note again and again and seek the satisfaction of the mind himself; in this work haste is the enemy. So if in one sitting one brings out even half a line of a song and practises it, playing it again and again and matching it with the mental picture, then by doing so one will have more success in bringing out the next line. Those who bring out a whole song wrongly in one go and play it, their intelligence becomes displeased with them, and they cannot make themselves [their own] guru. So they always have to depend on some other guru.

(4) When one line of a song has come out on the bānsurī, write the svarāntara saṅkhyā (interval number) in place of the dots put on the mātrās of the syllables of the written words, so that the distance from one syllable to the next is understood exactly and is useful later too. Just as someone who enters his dark house gropes with his hands for a lamp and the like, lights it, and then uses other things in the light, in the same way the practitioner too makes (tamaso mā jyotirgamaya) [lead me from darkness to light] come true.
